items.followUp: Why are viruses considered non-living outside a host but living inside a host?

rubric.why: Shows the non-living condition of a virus outside its host.
rubric.description: States that viruses are inert or inactive outside a living host.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viruses are inactive or inert outside the host.

rubric.why: Shows a living characteristic expressed by viruses inside a host.
rubric.description: States that viruses reproduce or multiply inside living host cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viruses reproduce or multiply inside a host.

modelAnswer: Outside a living host, viruses are inert and do not carry out life activities.
Inside a living host cell, they reproduce and show living characteristics.

items.followUp: State two more principles of the cell theory.

accept: all living things are made of cells
all organisms are made of cells
rubric.why: This is a principle of cell theory about the cellular composition of living things.
rubric.description: States that living organisms are composed of one or more cells.

accept: cells arise from pre existing cells
new cells arise from existing cells
rubric.why: Either statement is another accepted principle of cell theory.
rubric.description: States that the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, or that new cells arise from pre-existing cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either principle, provided it is distinct from the first stated principle.

modelAnswer: All living organisms are composed of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

items.followUp: Differentiate between active transport and facilitated diffusion.

accept: particles move from higher concentration to lower concentration
movement from high concentration to low concentration
rubric.why: This describes the direction of diffusion down a concentration gradient.
rubric.description: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for its direction of movement.

rubric.why: Osmosis specifically involves water moving through a selectively permeable membrane.
rubric.description: Osmosis is the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution towards a more concentrated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water and its movement through a selectively permeable membrane.

modelAnswer: Diffusion is the movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration; it can occur in gases and liquids.
Osmosis is the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution towards a more concentrated solution.

items.followUp: What happens to a cell during apoptosis?

rubric.why: Apoptotic bodies are formed as membrane-bound fragments during programmed cell death.
rubric.description: Identifies apoptotic bodies as small membrane-bound fragments or vesicles formed from a cell undergoing apoptosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing their formation and membrane-bound nature.

rubric.why: The bodies are removed by engulfment after they form.
rubric.description: States that apoptotic bodies are engulfed or phagocytosed by other cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing their removal.

modelAnswer: During apoptosis, the cell breaks into small membrane-bound fragments called apoptotic bodies.
These bodies are engulfed by neighbouring cells or phagocytes.

items.followUp: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur, and between which chromatids?

rubric.why: Crossing over involves the exchange of genetic material.
rubric.description: Defines crossing over as the exchange of genetic material or chromosome segments.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the exchange.

rubric.why: The exchange occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I.
rubric.description: Identifies the chromatids or the stage of meiosis involved.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes or prophase I (pachytene).

modelAnswer: Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
It occurs during prophase I of meiosis.

items.followUp: Name two enzymes that digest food in the human digestive system.

rubric.why: Any correctly named enzyme earns credit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid enzyme name.

rubric.why: A second correctly named enzyme earns the second mark.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid enzyme different from the first.

items.followUp: Explain how the active site changes when a substrate binds according to the induced fit model.

rubric.why: The induced fit model proposes that the active site is flexible rather than a rigid, exact fit before binding.
rubric.description: States that the enzyme's active site changes shape or is not exactly complementary to the substrate before binding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the initial flexibility or shape change of the active site.

rubric.why: The change brings the active site into a fit with the substrate and forms the enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.description: States that substrate binding induces a change so the active site fits the substrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the induced fit after substrate binding.

modelAnswer: In the induced fit model, the enzyme's active site is not exactly complementary to the substrate before binding.
When the substrate binds, the active site changes shape to fit it and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.

items.followUp: Who discovered ATP, and in which year?

rubric.why: Identifies the scientist credited with discovering ATP.
rubric.description: Names Karl Lohmann as the discoverer of ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct name.

rubric.why: Identifies the year ATP was discovered.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct year.

modelAnswer: ATP was discovered by Karl Lohmann in 1929.
